solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Pain in court gaining favour

indicators.note: one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside it

blocks.note: an ache is a dull pain
CT is the standard abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: Someone suffers in a law court while trying to win the judge's approval.
explanation.walkthrough: The pain goes inside the abbreviation for court; 'gaining' simply links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cachet is prestige or social approval, close in sense to standing in someone's good favour.

clue.text: Cleaner source of energy for another

blocks.note: a char, or charwoman, is a cleaning lady
coal is a fuel burnt for energy

explanation.surface: A greener fuel is proposed as a replacement for a dirtier one.
explanation.walkthrough: A char is a British cleaning lady. The second half of the wordplay doubles as part of the definition: the answer is a fuel standing in for that other fuel.
explanation.definitionFit: Charcoal is burnt as a fuel in place of wood or mineral coal, so it is one energy source substituted for a different one.

clue.text: Chuck out project over digression

blocks.note: to cast is to throw or project, as an image or a line
an aside is a remark that wanders off the main subject

explanation.surface: A manager scraps a project because it has wandered off on a tangent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'project' reads as a noun but works as the verb to throw; in a down clue 'over' places the first part above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To chuck something out is to discard it, which is exactly what rejecting or dumping something entails.

clue.text: Ben Hur, say, is in the pictures

indicators.note: something that is in a phrase sits inside its run of letters

blocks.note: spans the last letter of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A film buff notes that the chariot-racing hero has made it onto the big screen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the pictures' is an old British name for the cinema, so the clue reads as a plain statement; Ben-Hur (1959) is the classic grand historical film.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, lavish historical film with huge sets and casts is the standard example of this film genre.

clue.text: Blasted rugged

blocks.note: first meaning: severely told off, as a boss calls someone onto the carpet
second meaning: covered with rugs, read literally as rug-ged

explanation.walkthrough: 'rugged' looks like the adjective for rough terrain; here it means furnished with rugs. Being carpeted is British slang for a dressing-down.
explanation.definitionFit: A reprimanded employee has been hauled over the coals, and a floor laid with rugs has floor covering on it.

clue.text: Early style of facility cracking code

indicators.note: something cracked has been broken apart, so its letters fall into a new order

blocks.note: art is skill or knack, a facility for doing something
taken as written

explanation.surface: A codebreaking facility is credited with an early approach to its work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'facility' suggests a building but means a skill. The style dates from the 1920s and 1930s, hence 'early' in twentieth-century terms.
explanation.definitionFit: The geometric decorative movement of the interwar years is an early modern design style in architecture and furnishing.

clue.text: Sit with pal wriggling and bear sculpture, for example

indicators.note: something wriggling twists about, so these letters squirm into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of both words, taken together
to cart is to carry or bear a load

explanation.surface: A child fidgets beside a friend while posing next to a statue of a bear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bear' looks like the animal in the sculpture but is the verb to carry.
explanation.definitionFit: Visual arts that shape materials in three dimensions, such as modelling and carving statues, are grouped under this heading.

clue.text: Pulse among British

blocks.note: thro' is a poetic shortening of through, as in passing among things
B is the abbreviation for British

explanation.walkthrough: 'among' looks like a container signal but supplies letters itself: the old clipped spelling of through.
explanation.definitionFit: A pulse is a regular beating, and a heart that beats strongly is said to pound or pulsate rhythmically.

clue.text: Tranquilizer dart’s first keeper

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter alone

blocks.note: the opening letter of dart
an owner keeps or holds something as their own

explanation.surface: A zookeeper is the first target of a tranquilliser dart.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a zoo, but 'keeper' is simply someone who possesses something.
explanation.definitionFit: A downer is slang for a sedative drug that calms the nervous system, the class of pill a tranquilliser belongs to.

clue.text: Speak about fair cut for security

indicators.note: something cut has been trimmed, losing its tail end
to be about something is to surround it on all sides

blocks.note: to say is to speak
a fete is a fair; cut short it loses its final E

explanation.surface: A speaker argues for a fair reduction in the interest of security.
explanation.walkthrough: A fete is a village fair or garden party, common in Britain; the shortened version sits inside the word for speak.
explanation.definitionFit: Security and safety both mean freedom from danger or harm, so the two nouns are close synonyms.

clue.text: One attacks clot to upset social worker?

blocks.note: a clot is a fool, as is an ass
to ail is to trouble or upset someone
an ant is a worker that lives in a colony, a social insect

explanation.surface: Someone lashes out at a fool for upsetting a social worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'social worker' sounds like a job in care; it is the insect. 'Clot' is British slang for an idiot. The definition is a clause: a person who attacks.
explanation.definitionFit: An assailant is a person who assaults someone, so the noun describes whoever carries out the violence.

clue.text: Missile is limited once head’s defused

indicators.note: defusing removes a warhead, so the word loses its front letter

blocks.note: narrow means restricted or limited in scope

explanation.surface: A rocket's danger is reduced once its warhead has been made safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' in the surface is a warhead; in the wordplay it is the first letter of the word for limited.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrow is a projectile shot from a bow, the oldest kind of missile launched at a target.

clue.text: Fellow’s chosen sportsperson, hard to be contained

indicators.note: something contained is held inside something else

blocks.note: a cap is a player selected for a national team
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A man's chosen athlete is a tough character who must be kept in check.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a player picked for the national side is said to win a cap, and the player is called a cap.
explanation.definitionFit: Chap is informal British English for a man, the same as calling him a fellow or a bloke.

clue.text: Pleasing daughter with a good chance of getting in

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter

blocks.clueFragment: with a good chance of getting in
blocks.note: a candidate likely to win a vote, getting into office

explanation.surface: A parent is pleased that their daughter is likely to win a place, at a school perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting in' suggests admission to a school or club; it means winning an election.
explanation.definitionFit: Delectable means delightful or delicious, giving pleasure to the senses, so pleasing is a looser synonym.

clue.text: French division knocking back gin with me in depression

indicators.note: knocking back a drink tips it backwards, so the word runs the other way
one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: a gin is a snare or trap for animals
taken as written
a dent is a hollow or depression in a surface

explanation.surface: A Frenchman drowns his sorrows by knocking back gin while feeling low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gin' looks like the drink, and 'knocking back' fits it, but gin is also an old word for a snare. France is divided into administrative areas called départements.
explanation.definitionFit: France's main administrative regions are called départements, so the English word names one of those regional units.

clue.text: Supply one in busy galley

indicators.note: a busy place is full of bustle and movement, so the letters are moved about

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cook hands out provisions in a crowded ship's kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like the verb or noun for providing; here it is the adverb from supple, pronounced supple-ee, meaning nimbly.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving in a supple way means bending and moving nimbly, which is exactly how someone nimble moves.

clue.text: Larger than the average motors getting awards

blocks.note: OS is the clothing-size abbreviation for outsize
motor is a British informal word for a car

explanation.surface: Bigger-than-usual vehicles win prizes, perhaps at a motor show.
explanation.walkthrough: OS marks outsize garments in British shops.
explanation.definitionFit: The Academy Awards for film achievement are popularly known by the nickname of their gold statuette.

clue.text: New uni in helping downfall

indicators.note: something new has been remade, so the letters take a fresh order
one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
a ration is a portion or helping of food

explanation.surface: A new university is blamed for helping to bring about someone's collapse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'helping' reads as a verb but is the noun for a serving of food.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruination is the state of being ruined, and a downfall is likewise a collapse of fortune or status.

clue.text: Pointless and pretty much blunt soaps

indicators.note: pretty much means almost all, so the word stops short of its last letter

blocks.note: a flat joke or remark has no point
blunt and terse both describe curt, abrupt speech

explanation.surface: A critic dismisses television soap operas as pointless and dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soaps' looks like a plural noun for TV dramas; it is the verb, as in to soft-soap someone.
explanation.definitionFit: To soft-soap someone is to win them over with smooth praise, so the verb means to butter up or compliment insincerely.

clue.text: Smooth delicate fabric back in British Museum

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the word is turned round
one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: lace is a fine openwork fabric
BM is the standard abbreviation for the British Museum

explanation.surface: A curator smooths out a fragile old textile on display in a London museum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smooth' looks like an adjective but is a verb: to still or make calm, as when a ship is left without wind.
explanation.definitionFit: To becalm is to make still or quiet, as the sea is smoothed when the wind drops.

clue.text: Decency from kind pen

blocks.note: a mode is a kind, form or manner of something
a sty is a pen for pigs

explanation.surface: Good manners shown in a gentle letter from a considerate writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kind' looks like an adjective and 'pen' like a writing tool; they are a noun for type and an animal enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: Modesty is propriety in dress and behaviour, a sense of seemliness that matches decency.

clue.text: Warlike poet of old

blocks.note: first meaning: of or suited to war
second meaning: the first-century Roman writer of epigrams

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests an ancient bard who sang of battle; the Roman epigrammatist is a separate meaning of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective comes from Mars, the Roman god of war, and the Latin satirist Marcus Valerius Martialis is known in English by the same name.

clue.text: Being time to go into teaching?

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it

blocks.note: the moral of a story is its teaching or lesson
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether it is time to enter the teaching profession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'teaching' suggests the job; it is the lesson of a fable. 'Being' looks like a verb but is the noun for a living creature.
explanation.definitionFit: A mortal is a human creature subject to death, so a living person is a being in that sense.

clue.text: Wolf ignoring cold round fruit

indicators.note: to ignore something is to leave it out of account

blocks.note: a wolf, a womaniser, is also called a tomcat
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps; this C is removed
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A hungry wolf, unbothered by the cold, goes after a round piece of fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wolf' looks like the animal or the verb to eat greedily; it is a man who chases women. The cold is the second C, not the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Botanically the tomato is a fruit, the seed-bearing part of the plant, though it is usually eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Old boy squirts spring in valuable items

blocks.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil
jets are squirts of liquid
to dart is to spring or dash suddenly

explanation.surface: A former pupil hides fountain-like water squirts among some precious possessions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spring' suggests water, fitting the squirts, but it is the verb for leaping. An old boy is a British school's former pupil.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means small decorative objects of artistic worth, the kind of precious ornaments people collect.

clue.text: Support is in hint

indicators.note: one thing in another is placed inside it

blocks.note: a jot is a tiny amount, a hint of something
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone says their help lies in merely making a suggestion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Support' reads as moral backing; it is a structural beam.
explanation.definitionFit: A joist is one of the parallel timber or steel beams that hold up a floor or ceiling, a structural support.

clue.text: Answer is in a little temptation

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it

blocks.note: a bit is a little amount
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: The solution to a craving is to give in to it just a little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a little' must be read whole as a noun phrase, not as 'a' plus a separate adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Bait is something used to lure or entice, so it is an enticement or lure that tempts.

clue.text: Actual solid houses too

indicators.note: a house holds things inside it, so the word sits within the letters

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Real, substantial homes are being described, too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'houses' looks like a plural noun but is the verb to contain.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean in addition or as well, and each can end a sentence in the same way.

clue.text: Appear as a gent backing environment primarily

indicators.note: backing means moving in reverse, so the word runs the other way
primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter is wanted

blocks.note: taken as written
a sir is a gentleman, as in a polite form of address
the opening letter of environment

explanation.surface: A man turns up as a supporter of green causes above all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing' suggests supporting a cause; it turns the title round.
explanation.definitionFit: To arise is to come into being or emerge, so when a problem arises it appears or crops up.

clue.text: Insignificant beginning to some shopping experience?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of some
hours spent at a shopping centre, time at the mall

explanation.surface: A trivial start to a day out shopping.
explanation.walkthrough: A mall is an American-style shopping centre. The question mark admits that the second phrase is invented.
explanation.definitionFit: A small-time crook or operator is minor and unimportant, working on a petty scale.

clue.text: Bottled stout, say, lasts longer

indicators.note: bottled is slang for drunk, and a drunk staggers about out of order

blocks.note: the letters of both words, taken together

explanation.surface: Bottled beer such as stout keeps for longer than draught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' looks like the usual signal that stout is just one example of a beer, but its letters are part of the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: To outstay is to remain somewhere beyond another person or a limit, staying on beyond the usual time.

clue.text: Establishes means holds nothing

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside

blocks.note: a person's means are their money or funds
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A business is set up with funds that turn out to contain nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'means' reads as a verb but is the noun for money.
explanation.definitionFit: To found a company or institution is to set it up and bring it into being, which is to establish it.
